nameStory: The Eastern Tent Caterpillar gets its name from the silky white tents these social caterpillars weave together in tree branches, looking like camping tents pitched in the forest canopy. These communal shelters protect the young caterpillars as they grow, and you'll often see dozens of fuzzy caterpillars emerging from a single tent to feed on nearby leaves.
description: The Eastern Tent Caterpillar Moth is a fuzzy, brown moth that most people encounter first as colorful caterpillars living in silky white tents in cherry and apple trees. The adult moths are relatively plain with brownish wings, but the caterpillars are the real showstoppers - covered in soft hairs with striking blue, white, black, and orange markings running down their backs. These social caterpillars work together to build communal silk tents where they shelter between feeding sessions. The moths produce one generation per year, making their tents a reliable spring sight in New England.

idTips.label: Silky White Tent
idTips.description: Look for distinctive white silk tents woven into the forks of tree branches, feeling smooth and papery to the touch when abandoned later in the season

idTips.label: Colorful Caterpillars
idTips.description: Fuzzy caterpillars with soft, velvety hair and a distinctive pattern of blue spots, white stripes, and orange-red markings along their black bodies

idTips.label: Host Trees
idTips.description: Almost always found on cherry, apple, and other trees in the rose family - if you see tents on oak or other trees, it's likely a different species

idTips.label: Group Behavior
idTips.description: Caterpillars travel together in long lines like a fuzzy parade, often dozens moving single-file along branches to and from their tent

idTips.label: Adult Moth
idTips.description: Brown, fuzzy-bodied moths with two pale diagonal stripes across each forewing, attracted to lights on summer evenings

habitat: Throughout New England wherever wild cherry, apple, and other rose family trees grow - from suburban yards and orchards to forest edges and old fields. They're particularly common along woodland borders where wild black cherry trees thrive, and you'll often spot their tents in abandoned apple orchards or even ornamental cherry trees in town centers.

seasonality.spring: Peak tent-building season when young caterpillars emerge and create their distinctive white silk shelters in tree forks, most visible in April and May.
seasonality.summer: Adult moths emerge and are active at night, attracted to porch lights and laying eggs on tree bark. Old tents may still be visible as weathered silk remnants.
seasonality.fall: Egg masses are laid on twigs as dark, shiny bands that encircle small branches. Moths have finished their life cycle and tents are long abandoned.
seasonality.winter: Only the egg masses survive, appearing as dark, varnish-like bands wrapped around cherry and apple tree twigs.

funFact: The brilliant blue color on tent caterpillars isn't from pigment at all - it's created by microscopic tubes in their skin that filter light like tiny prisms, making them living jewels that literally bend light to create their dazzling blue spots.
confusionNotes: Often confused with Fall Webworms (which build tents at branch tips in late summer) and Gypsy Moth caterpillars (which don't build tents at all). Remember: Eastern Tent Caterpillars build their white tents in the forks of branches in spring, while webworms tent the ends of branches in fall.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'pests' by some gardeners, these native moths are an important food source for over 60 bird species. The caterpillars rarely cause lasting damage to healthy trees, and their population naturally cycles up and down over several years.
compareHints: The closely related Forest Tent Caterpillar doesn't actually build tents despite its name, and has keyhole-shaped white markings instead of blue spots. Eastern Tent Caterpillars are the tent-builders with blue spots, while Forest Tent Caterpillars gather in groups on tree trunks without tents and sport distinctive white 'keyhole' patterns down their backs.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Forest Tent Caterpillars differ from their close relative, the Eastern Tent Caterpillar, in several key ways: they have white diamond spots instead of a solid white stripe down the back, they make flat silk resting mats rather than enclosed tent structures, and they tend to feed higher in the forest canopy.
